member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateNamedPoolCollection`1
member.summary: Holds every named pool of one element type: the lazily built singletons behind the declarations in the container.
member.remarks:
A pool is built on the first request for its name and then reused, so declaring a pool costs nothing until something asks for it — and asking twice never builds twice. Names that were never requested stay unbuilt, which is what makes "declare a pool per tenant" affordable.
The collection owns the pools it built and disposes them when the container is disposed; a pool that was never requested is never created and therefore never disposed.

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.HayateNamedPoolRegistration`1
member.summary: A named-pool declaration: the service key a pool is addressed by, plus the delegate that builds it when it is first asked for.
member.remarks: Named pools are deliberately not built on Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection keyed services: those only exist in version 8.0 and later of the abstractions package, so a keyed registration would be unavailable to the net6.0 / net7.0 targets this library ships. A named pool is therefore declared as one instance of this type in the container — the container's own "many registrations of one service type" facility, available on every supported target — and collects them. The observable behavior is the same on net48 through net10.0: one lazily built singleton per (type, name).

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.IHayateNamedPoolAccessor
member.summary: Resolves named pools — and the single unnamed pool of a type — from the container.
member.remarks:
A pool registered with RegisterHayatePool<T>() is resolvable as directly; that stops working as soon as a second pool of the same type exists, because there is then no longer one answer to "the pool of T". Named pools are addressed through this accessor instead, which is what a typed client uses and what an application asks when it wants a specific pool by name.
Resolution never creates a pool: it returns what was registered, and throws when the name was never registered. Run-time creation is 's job, so a typo in a pool name surfaces as an error rather than silently starting an unconfigured pool.

member.remarks:
The pool is registered under the canonical name {typeof(T).Name}:{name} — see — so the management endpoints can tell the pools apart in logs, statistics and snapshots. It is built on first use rather than at registration time, and it is resolved through (or injected into a typed client via ) rather than as , which stays reserved for the unnamed pool.
Declaring the same name twice keeps the last declaration, as repeated DI registrations do.
